q: You're driving slowly along a residential street. An ice-cream van is parked on the left ahead. What's the main hazard you should be ready for?
options: Children running out into the road
The van sounding its chimes
Traffic lights hidden behind it
The van switching its lights on
explain: Drive carefully and slowly when passing parked vehicles, especially ice-cream vans. Children are more interested in ice cream than traffic and may run into the road unexpectedly.

q: You're driving along a narrow street lined with parked cars. You notice someone sitting in the driver's seat of one of them. What should you be prepared for?
options: Its alarm going off
Its horn being sounded at you
A door opening into your path
Its hazard lights coming on
explain: On streets with parked cars you should drive slowly and carefully. Look out for car doors opening, vehicles moving off and children running out from between parked cars.

q: You're driving through a town and see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: No cycling allowed ahead
A cycle route ahead
A cycle-only lane ahead
A cycle parking area ahead
explain: This triangular warning sign shows a cycle route ahead. Look out for cyclists, who can be difficult to see, especially at junctions.

q: You're approaching a bus that has stopped at a bus stop on your side of the road. What should you look out for in particular?
options: The bus switching on its hazard lights
Its exhaust fumes blocking your view
The bus driver waving you past
People stepping out in front of it
explain: Drive carefully and slowly past bus stops, as pedestrians may emerge suddenly into the road. Look out for people getting off a bus and crossing the road.

q: You're driving near a school. There's a flashing amber signal below the 'School' warning sign. What should you do?
options: Drive very slowly until you're clear of the area
Stop and wait until the signal stops flashing
Keep to the speed limit and cover your brake
Sound your horn to warn children you're there
explain: A flashing amber signal below the 'School' warning sign tells you there may be children crossing the road ahead. Drive very slowly until you're clear of the area.

q: You're approaching a school crossing patrol waiting at the kerb. A slow-moving van is in front of you. What should you do?
options: Overtake it before you reach the patrol
Stay behind it and don't overtake
Overtake if no children are in view
Sound your horn to warn the patrol
explain: Don't overtake where you might come into conflict with other road users, such as when approaching a school crossing patrol. You MUST stop if the patrol shows a 'Stop for children' sign.

q: You're driving along a street with a tramway. A tram is approaching a stop ahead. What should you look out for?
options: Cars racing the tram from the lights
The tram changing to a different lane
People running to catch the tram
Cyclists riding along the rails
explain: Look out for pedestrians, especially children, running to catch a tram approaching a stop. Also look out for people getting off a tram and crossing the road.

q: You're driving along a country road. Why should you slow down as you approach junctions and turnings?
options: They may be partially hidden
They always have a stop line
Traffic in them must give way to you
They're always on sharp bends
explain: On country roads, reduce your speed at junctions and turnings, which may be partially hidden, and on the approach to bends, which can be sharper than they appear.

q: You're following a powered mobility scooter on the road. Its user wants to turn right, but moving into the middle of the road would be dangerous. What might they do?
options: Stop in the middle of the road and wait
Signal left and then turn right
Speed up to get ahead of the traffic
Stop on the left and wait for a safe gap
explain: If moving into the middle of the road is difficult or dangerous, a mobility scooter user may stop on the left-hand side of the road and wait for a safe gap, or make the turn as a pedestrian. Be patient and give them room.

q: You're waiting to emerge from a side road. A car approaching from the right is signalling left, as if to turn into your road. What should you do?
options: Pull out, as the car is turning in
Wait until you're sure it's turning
Flash your headlights to let it in
Pull out quickly before it reaches you
explain: When waiting at a junction, don't assume that a vehicle coming from the right and signalling left will actually turn. Wait and make sure, as its indicator may not have been cancelled.

q: The car in front has been showing a right-turn signal for some distance but hasn't turned. You want to overtake it. What should you do?
options: Overtake it on the right quickly
Flash your headlights, then overtake
Stay behind until the signal is cancelled
Sound your horn as you overtake
explain: Don't overtake when a road user is indicating right, even if you believe the signal should have been cancelled. Don't take a risk; wait for the signal to be cancelled.

q: You're in slow-moving traffic approaching a pedestrian crossing. Queuing vehicles are blocking your view of the pavement on both sides. Why should you take extra care?
options: People may be crossing between the vehicles
The crossing may be closed to pedestrians
Drivers behind may sound their horns
The road surface may be slippery
explain: Take extra care where the view of either side of a crossing is blocked by queuing traffic or incorrectly parked vehicles. Pedestrians may be crossing between stationary vehicles.

q: You're following a large lorry on a single carriageway road. How can you improve your view of the road ahead?
options: Drop back to increase the gap
Move closer so you can see past it
Switch your headlights to main beam
Drive with your wheels on the centre line
explain: Large vehicles can block your view. Your ability to see and to plan ahead will be improved if you pull back to increase your separation distance.

q: You're following an articulated lorry along a busy road. Why should you keep well back?
options: So you can read its number plate
So you're clear of its exhaust fumes
So it can't reverse into you
So the driver can see you in the mirrors
explain: If you're following a large vehicle, be aware that the driver may not be able to see you in the mirrors. Dropping back should allow the driver to see you, and it also improves your view ahead.

q: You're driving through a hilly area and see this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: Rocks on the road ahead
A steep drop at the roadside
Loose chippings from road works
Low-flying aircraft overhead
explain: This sign warns of falling or fallen rocks. Be prepared for rocks on the road and drive at a speed that lets you stop well within the distance you can see to be clear.

q: You're driving along a country road and see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: Road humps
Uneven road
Hump bridge
Steep hill upwards
explain: This sign warns of a hump bridge. You can't see far enough ahead as you approach a hump bridge to be sure it's safe, so don't overtake there.

q: You're driving along a country road and see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A zebra crossing ahead
Pedestrians in the road ahead
A school entrance ahead
A footbridge over the road
explain: This sign warns of pedestrians in the road ahead, for example where there's no pavement. Slow down, be prepared to stop and give them plenty of room as you pass.

q: You've been driving in thick fog, which now seems to be clearing. What should you be aware of?
options: You can speed up to make up lost time
You may suddenly find yourself in thick fog
You can close up to the vehicle ahead
You can ignore any further 'Fog' signs
explain: Even if fog seems to be clearing, you can suddenly find yourself in thick fog. Keep a safe distance and make sure you can pull up well within the distance you can see clearly.

q: You're driving on a country road and see this sign. What should you do?
options: Keep to the right on the bend
Reduce your speed before the bend
Brake firmly while on the bend
Overtake before you reach the bend
explain: This sign warns of a bend to the right. On country roads, reduce your speed on the approach to bends, which can be sharper than they appear. Keep well to the left on right-hand bends to improve your view.

q: You see this sign. What should you do?
options: Keep your speed and brake hard if needed
Speed up to get through it quickly
Slow down and avoid harsh braking
Steer sharply round the slippery parts
explain: This sign warns of a slippery road. Skidding is usually caused by braking, accelerating or steering too harshly, or by driving too fast for the road conditions.

q: You're driving on a motorway and the vehicle in front switches on its hazard warning lights, as shown. What does this tell you?
options: The driver is about to change lanes
There's a hazard or obstruction ahead
The driver is leaving at the next exit
The vehicle is towing a trailer
explain: On a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway, drivers may briefly use hazard warning lights to warn drivers behind of a hazard or obstruction ahead. Be ready to slow down.
ref: HC Signals to other road users

q: You're driving through road works. Part of the road has been marked off by traffic cones, but nobody seems to be working there. What should you do?
options: Drive through it to pass the queue
Use it if the lane beside it is busy
Drive through it slowly and carefully
Keep out of the coned-off area
explain: Do not drive through an area marked off by traffic cones. Areas marked off by cones can contain significant hazards.

q: Farm animals are often herded along the country roads where you live. What may the herders do to warn traffic, especially near a bend?
options: Send someone ahead along the road
Set up temporary traffic lights
Park a tractor across the road
Put warning triangles on the verge
explain: People herding animals should, if possible, send another person along the road in front to warn other road users, especially at a bend or the brow of a hill. Look out for animals being driven on the road and be ready to stop.

q: You're driving at night on a road with no pavement. Ahead, a red light is being carried by someone walking in the road on your side. What could it be?
options: The front of an organised group of walkers
The rear of an organised group of walkers
A person directing traffic at an incident
A broken-down car's hazard light
explain: Organised walks on a road without a pavement should keep to the left. At night, the look-out in front should show a white light and the one at the back a red light. Slow down and give them plenty of room.

q: You're driving across open moorland on an unfenced road and see this sign. What should you be prepared for?
options: Animals being herded along the road
A riding school entrance ahead
Wild animals on the road
A cattle grid across the road
explain: This sign warns of wild animals. Watch out for animals on unfenced roads: drive slowly, give them plenty of room and be ready to stop.

q: You see this sign. What does it warn you about?
options: Wild horses or ponies
A horse racing course ahead
A stables entrance ahead
Accompanied horses or ponies
explain: This sign warns of accompanied horses or ponies on the road. When you see a horse, slow down and, when it's safe, pass wide and slowly.

q: You're driving along a winding country lane. Which of these should you be prepared to find on the road?
options: Trams crossing the road
Vehicles using a hard shoulder
Zig-zag lines on the bends
Mud on the road surface
explain: Take extra care on country roads. Be prepared for pedestrians, horse riders, cyclists, slow-moving farm vehicles or mud on the road surface, and make sure you can stop within the distance you can see to be clear.

q: You're driving along a country lane with no pavement. Where are pedestrians advised to walk?
options: On the right, facing oncoming traffic
On the left, with their backs to traffic
In the middle of the lane
On whichever side has more room
explain: If there's no pavement, pedestrians are advised to keep to the right-hand side of the road so they can see oncoming traffic. Expect walkers coming towards you on your side of the road.

q: You're driving at night on an unlit road. Why should you drive more slowly than you would in daylight?
options: Speed limits are lower at night
Your brakes work less well in the dark
Other drivers must dip their headlights
It's harder to see other road users
explain: You should reduce your speed when driving at night, as it's more difficult to see other road users. Drive at a speed that will allow you to stop well within the distance you can see to be clear.

q: You're thinking about overtaking a slow-moving van at night. Why do you need to take extra care?
options: It's harder to judge speed and distance
Overtaking isn't allowed after dark
You must use main beam as you pass
The van driver can't see your lights
explain: Take extra care when overtaking at night and in poor visibility, when it's harder to judge speed and distance. Keep your headlights dipped until you're level with the other vehicle.

q: You're driving towards a low, bright sun and it's dazzling you. What should you do?
options: Slow down, and stop if necessary
Speed up to get out of the glare
Switch on your rear fog lights
Look at the kerb and keep going
explain: If you're dazzled by bright sunlight, slow down and, if necessary, stop.

q: It's been raining heavily. How will your stopping distance compare with the distance on a dry road?
options: It'll be about the same
It'll be up to half as much again
It'll be at least double
It'll be ten times greater
explain: In wet weather, stopping distances will be at least double those required for stopping on dry roads, because your tyres have less grip on the road. They can be ten times greater on icy roads.

q: You're driving along a town street. The pavement ahead is closed for street repairs. What should you be prepared for?
options: Traffic lights that aren't working
Pedestrians walking in the road
Cyclists riding on the closed pavement
Buses stopping in the middle of the road
explain: Drive carefully and slowly when the pavement is closed due to street repairs, as pedestrians may be directed to use the road.

q: You're driving on a cold winter's day. The roads have been gritted, but there are icy patches about. What should you be prepared for?
options: Normal grip, as the road has been treated
Shorter stopping distances than usual
Conditions changing over short distances
Ice only on the busiest stretches of road
explain: In icy or snowy weather, drive with care even if the roads have been treated, and be prepared for the road conditions to change over relatively short distances.

q: There's snow and ice on the roads and you want to check how much grip your tyres have. What should you do?
options: Accelerate hard on a straight stretch
Brake gently in a safe place
Steer sharply from side to side
Brake hard at a moderate speed
explain: When there's snow or ice, check your grip on the road surface by choosing a safe place to brake gently. If the steering feels unresponsive, this may indicate ice and that your vehicle is losing its grip.

q: A recovery vehicle is helping a broken-down car at the side of the road ahead. Why should you drive carefully and slowly as you pass?
options: Recovery vehicles always have priority
People may be working in or beside the road
The law sets a 10 mph limit when passing
You MUST stop until it has moved off
explain: Drive carefully and slowly when passing roadside rescue and recovery vehicles or going through road works, as there may be people working in or at the side of the road.

q: You're driving in thick fog, closely following the rear lights of the car in front. Why could this be dangerous?
options: They give a false sense of security
They'll stop you seeing road signs
They'll make the fog seem thicker
They mean you can't use your headlights
explain: When driving in fog, keep a safe distance behind the vehicle in front, as rear lights can give a false sense of security. Make sure you can pull up well within the distance you can see clearly.

q: You're driving through road works with a temporary 40 mph speed limit. The road looks clear and nobody seems to be working. What MUST you do?
options: Return to the road's normal speed limit
Keep to the temporary speed limit
Exceed it, as no workers are present
Treat the limit as advice only
explain: At road works, take extra care and observe all signs; they're there for your safety and the safety of road workers. You MUST NOT exceed any temporary maximum speed limit.

q: You're driving through road works and there's a lot of activity in the works area beside you. Where should your attention be?
options: On the machinery in the works area
On the road ahead
On your mirrors the whole time
On your satnav for a quicker route
explain: At road works, concentrate on the road ahead, not the road works. Bear in mind the road ahead may be obstructed by the works or by slow-moving or stationary traffic.

q: You're approaching road works on a dual carriageway and see this sign. What does it show?
options: The hard shoulder is closed for road works
One lane crossover at contraflow road works
Two lanes merge into one at road works
The end of the road works and restrictions
explain: This sign shows a one-lane crossover at contraflow road works. In a contraflow you may be in a narrower lane than normal, with no permanent barrier between you and oncoming traffic.

q: You're driving past road works. A works vehicle showing flashing amber lights is travelling in the road ahead of you. What should you do?
options: Overtake it as soon as you can
Follow it closely through the works
Flash your lights so it pulls in
Leave extra space behind it
explain: Where vehicles are travelling in the road at road works and displaying amber warning lights, leave extra space and expect them to slow or turn into a works area.

q: You're driving along a busy street and see this sign. What should you be ready to do?
options: Give way to traffic at a roundabout
Stop at a school crossing patrol
Stop for people at a zebra crossing
Give way to cyclists on a cycle route
explain: This sign warns of a zebra crossing ahead. Look out for pedestrians waiting to cross and be ready to slow down or stop to let them cross.

q: You see this sign on a country road. What does it tell you?
options: You're entering a one-way street
Overtaking is allowed ahead
There's a lay-by on the left
The road bends sharply ahead
explain: Chevron signs like this show a sharp deviation of route. Reduce your speed on the approach, as bends can be sharper than they appear.

q: You're waiting to turn at a junction and a horse rider is approaching. What should you be aware of?
options: They may take an unexpected line
They must keep close to the kerb
They'll always signal before turning
They have to give way to you
explain: Take extra care at junctions. Watch out for horse riders, who may take a different line on the road from the one you'd expect.

q: You're following a slow van and see this sign. Why shouldn't you overtake here?
options: There's a bend ahead
The road narrows ahead
There's a junction ahead
It's a one-way street
explain: This sign warns that the road narrows on both sides. Don't overtake where you might come into conflict with other road users, such as where the road narrows.

q: You're driving in England. What's the legal limit for alcohol in your breath?
options: 22 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
35 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
50 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
80 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
explain: In England and Wales you MUST NOT drive with a breath alcohol level higher than 35 microgrammes per 100 millilitres of breath. The limit is lower in Scotland.

q: You're driving in Scotland. What's the legal limit for alcohol in your breath?
options: 35 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
50 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
80 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
22 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath
explain: In Scotland the legal limits are lower than in the rest of the UK. You MUST NOT drive with a breath alcohol level higher than 22 microgrammes per 100 millilitres of breath.

q: In England and Wales, what's the legal limit for alcohol in your blood when driving?
options: 35 milligrammes per 100 ml of blood
50 milligrammes per 100 ml of blood
80 milligrammes per 100 ml of blood
107 milligrammes per 100 ml of blood
explain: In England and Wales you MUST NOT drive with a blood alcohol level of more than 80 milligrammes per 100 millilitres of blood. In Scotland the blood limit is 50 milligrammes.

q: You've had a couple of alcoholic drinks and feel fine. How could the alcohol affect your driving?
options: It'll speed up your reactions
It'll improve your judgement of distance
It won't affect you below the limit
It can give you false confidence
explain: Alcohol gives a false sense of confidence, reduces co-ordination, slows down reactions and affects judgement of speed, distance and risk. It reduces your driving ability even if you're below the legal limit.

q: You drank a lot of alcohol at a party last night. You need to drive to work early this morning. What should you bear in mind?
options: A cold shower will sober you up
You may still be unfit to drive
Strong coffee removes the alcohol
A night's sleep clears all the alcohol
explain: Alcohol takes time to leave your body. You may be unfit to drive in the morning after drinking the previous evening, or in the evening after drinking at lunchtime.

q: Which of these can make a difference to how alcohol affects you?
options: The size of your car's engine
How far you're planning to drive
Your stress levels at the time
Whether it's daytime or night-time
explain: The way alcohol affects you depends on your weight, age, sex and metabolism, the type and amount of alcohol, what you've eaten recently and your stress levels at the time. It's impossible to say exactly how many drinks will take you over the limit.

q: Your pharmacist tells you that a medicine you've been given may impair your driving. What should you do?
options: Don't drive while you're taking it
Drive only on quiet country roads
Drive, but take some extra breaks
Drive only during daylight hours
explain: You MUST NOT drive under the influence of drugs or medicine. Check with your doctor or pharmacist, and don't drive if you're advised that you may be impaired.

q: Why is it so dangerous to drive after taking illegal drugs?
options: They only affect your eyesight
They make you drive too slowly
They're only risky mixed with alcohol
Their effects are unpredictable
explain: Never take illegal drugs if you intend to drive. The effects are unpredictable, but can be even more severe than alcohol and result in fatal or serious road crashes.

q: A driver is convicted of driving with alcohol above the legal limit. What's the minimum period they MUST be disqualified for?
options: 6 months
3 months
12 months
2 years
explain: For serious offences such as drink-driving, the court MUST order disqualification. The minimum period is 12 months, and it may be longer for repeat offenders or where the alcohol level is high.

q: Why could even a small amount of an illegal drug put you over the legal limit for driving?
options: The limits are the same as for alcohol
Drug tests can't measure small amounts
The limits only apply to large doses
The limits are set at very low levels
explain: You MUST NOT drive with illegal drugs in your blood above specified limits. These have been set at very low levels, so even small amounts of use could put you over the limit.

q: You've bought some cold medicine from a shop without a prescription. How can you find out whether it may affect your driving?
options: Read the label
Assume it's safe as it wasn't prescribed
Take a dose and see how you feel
Check how much alcohol it contains
explain: Even over-the-counter medicines can affect your ability to drive safely. Read the label to see if they may affect your driving, and check with your doctor or pharmacist if you're unsure.

q: A police officer suspects that your eyesight may not meet the standard for driving. What can they do?
options: Let you drive on if you're wearing glasses
Require you to take an eyesight test
Only issue you with a warning letter
Ban you from driving on the spot
explain: You MUST be able to read a vehicle number plate, in good daylight, from 20 metres. The police have the power to require a driver to undertake an eyesight test.

q: You see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A ford across the road
A risk of flooding
A quayside or river bank
An opening bridge ahead
explain: This warning sign shows that there's a quayside or river bank ahead.

q: You're driving near an airfield and see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: An airport car park ahead
The route to an airport
A helicopter landing pad
Low-flying aircraft
explain: This warning sign means low-flying aircraft or sudden aircraft noise, which could startle you. On direction signs, an aircraft symbol shows the route to an airport.

q: Which of these eyesight conditions do you NOT need to tell the DVLA about?
options: A problem affecting both eyes
A problem with your only working eye
Double vision in both eyes
Being short-sighted
explain: You must tell DVLA about any eyesight problem that affects both eyes, or the remaining eye if you only have one. This doesn't include being short-sighted, long-sighted or colour blind.

q: You're approaching road works on a busy road. What should you bear in mind about the road ahead?
options: It may be blocked by queuing traffic
It will be clear once you pass the sign
The speed limit no longer applies
Workers will always wave you through
explain: At road works, take extra care and look for signs giving more instructions. Bear in mind that the road ahead may be obstructed by the works or by slow-moving or stationary traffic.

q: You're driving along a one-way street and see this sign. What does it tell you?
options: The road ahead is closed to traffic
Two-way traffic straight ahead
You must turn left at the junction
Traffic merges from the left ahead
explain: This sign warns of two-way traffic straight ahead. Be prepared for oncoming vehicles and keep to the left.

q: You see this sign. What does it warn you of?
options: A hump bridge on a narrow road
A level crossing with barriers
An opening or swing bridge
A low bridge with little headroom
explain: This sign warns of an opening or swing bridge ahead. Alternately flashing red lights at lifting bridges mean you MUST stop.

q: You're about to overtake a cyclist who's riding past a row of parked cars. Why might they be further out from the cars than you'd expect?
options: Because they must ride in mid-lane
Because they want you to wait behind
To ride over the drain covers
To keep clear of doors being opened
explain: Cyclists are advised to ride at least a door's width or 1 metre from parked cars for their own safety. Give them plenty of room when you overtake.

q: You've stopped at red traffic lights in slow traffic. Why should you check your mirrors and blind spots before moving off when they change?
options: A motorcyclist may be waiting alongside you
The driver behind may want to overtake you
Your brake lights might not be working
The lights might be about to change back
explain: It's often difficult to see motorcyclists and cyclists, especially when they're waiting alongside you, coming up from behind or filtering through traffic. Check your mirrors and blind spots carefully before moving off.
